newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Battered baht perks up, awaits dose of IMF medicine.
newsitem.headline: Battered baht perks up, awaits dose of IMF medicine.

text.p: Thailand's reeling baht regained some of its poise in the latter part of the week as the market eagerly awaited the outcome of Monday's mutilateral loan talks.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) lead talks include a number of interested countries and institutions who will discuss the possibility of joining in a financing package to support Thailand's economic stabilization program.
The market clearly has high hopes that a multi-billion dollar loan package will be forthcoming and that it will be the $12-15 billion the Thais have said they were looking for.
"In the near-term such a deal would give a lot of support for a stabilisation of the baht," Christa Marti, senior economist at UBS in Singapore, said on Friday
"Assuming the talks go well I can see a near-term stabilisation of the baht around the 32.00 level, although with a lot of volatility."
Despite its easier bias on Friday, the baht managed to firm throughout the latter part of the week as the market became a little more confident about Thailand's economic outlook.

On Tuesday, the authorities announced a sweeping austerity package which included moves to cut the current account deficit, a rise in value added tax and the suspension of more than half Thailand's troubled finance companies.
The number of finance companies whose operations were suspect came as somewhat of a surprise, but grasping the nettle in this way impressed the markets and the baht moved higher.
On Friday, the onshore rate was quoted at 31.200, down on Thursday's late 30.800 but well above last Friday's close of 33.000 before the austerity measures were announced.
"I wouldn't say the market is confident or even optimistic at this stage," said a European bank trader in Singapore.

"Very cautiously optimistic, I suppose would sum it up...It looks like the loan deal is on track but there really is a nasty mess to sort out in Thailand and it's going to be quite a while before we see funds return to the region."
Monday's talks will thrash out the biggest funding package for a single country since $40 billion was made available to Mexico after its crisis in 1995.
So on the economic front at least thing seem set resonably fair, but there is a niggling worry at the back of the market's mind and that is the political backdrop to the situation.
Austerity measures are always unpopular and the market is worried about a political backlash, so traders will be keeping a close eye on developments there in the coming days and weeks.
Traders said given Thailand's volatile political history of military coups, it is no surprise that at a time like this the market becomes nervous and rumours start to swirl.
"Political issues always influence the market and they are obviously having more impact now because it's a more sensitive period," said one Singapore based analyst.
"That's why we have seen some volatility in the markets and people will obviously keep half an eye on the political scene until this is all sorted out."

The market became jittery on Thursday after Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh and Thailand's two top financial officials met King Bhumibol Adulyadej for more than 2-1/2 hours, although a government spokesman said, "There was nothing special in the audience with the King."

Despite the jitters, analysts said the general feeling in the market was that nothing would happen on the political front in the near-term or before the loan package has been sorted out and things settle down on the economic front.
"I'm sure the Thai opposition (parties) realise that an upset on the political front now would put the IMF package in serious jeopardy," said the European bank trader.
